newsitem.title: USA: Silicon Graphics tops estimates, upbeat on 1998.
newsitem.headline: Silicon Graphics tops estimates, upbeat on 1998.

text.p: Computer workstation maker Silicon Graphics Inc. posted a strong gain in fiscal fourth quarter income Thursday, startling Wall Street after nearly two years of repeated quarterly shortfalls.
The company said it earned $102 million, or 56 cents a share, on sales of $1.2 billion. A year earlier, the company posted a loss of $48.7 million, or 30 cents a share, on sales of $977 million.
Wall Street had been expecting revenues around $1 billion.

Moreover, Chief Executive Officer Edward McCracken told Reuters in an interview he expects Silicon Graphics to be able to sustain the higher profit margins it achieved in the fourth quarter throughout its 1998 fiscal year.

The company, whose products are used in computer-intensive applications from complex weather modelling to special effects in movies, said revenue growth was balanced across all its business units and was driven especially by the success of its Octane workstation and Origin 2000 scalable server families.

Its profit, which was announced after the close of market trading, exceeded the 34 cents a share that Wall Street analysts surveyed by First Call had expected. In after-hours trading, its stock jumped to $23 a share from $19.44.

The favourable earnings report gave Silicon Graphics investors a welcome boost after a sweeping product transition over the last year had battered their shares and contributed to repeated earnings disappointments.

"This quarter was all about execution," McCracken said. "Our product transition is complete, we are shipping our entire product line...and, most importantly, the new products are finding strong acceptance with customers."
Analysts said investors were still likely to be wary of the stock after so many quarters of missing its projected results.

"Silicon Graphics is a low-expectation stock," said David Wu, an analyst at ABN AMRO Chicago Corp. "For seven consecutive quarters they haven't made their numbers. This time they more than made their numbers."
But Bob Herwick, of Herwick Capital, said the positive quarterly results demonstrate that improved management controls can help bring the company back to steady growth.
"I think what investors would like to see before they put a really big (value) on the stock is predictability," he said. "Ed understands that and that's what he's working on."

"I think the success of this quarter is it highlights the fact that a very substantial percentage of this company's business comes from products where they in effect have no meaningful competition," Herwick added of the high-end graphical workstations, servers and supercomputer systems.

The fourth-quarter result included pre-tax merger charges of $6 million related to the company's April 1996 acquisition of supercomputer maker Cray Research. That compared with charges of $120 million in the same quarter a year earlier related to the same transaction.

McCracken said the fourth quarter was the last in which it will report charges related to the Cray acquisition, although it will write off around $20 million in the current quarter related to acquisition of a 3-D Internet software firm. For the
year, Silicon Graphics earned $78.5 million, or 43 cents a share, on sales of $3.09 billion. A year earlier, the company earned $115 million, or 65 cents a share, on sales of $2.55 billion.
